description.summary: applications export their menus; the shell renders them

protocol.description:
On Trinix the menu bar belongs to the screen, not to the window. An application therefore does not draw its menus — it describes them, and the shell draws the menus of whichever window is active, at the top of the display, in one consistent style.
Why a Wayland protocol rather than D-Bus, which is what every previous global-menu implementation used:
A menu belongs to a *surface*, and D-Bus has no notion of one. The established designs work around that by exporting the menu on the bus and then using a Wayland (or X11) protocol anyway, purely to say which surface the bus name belongs to — so the D-Bus route costs two IPC mechanisms, two lifetimes to reconcile, and a window whose menus outlive it by however long the bus takes to notice. Carrying the model on the Wayland connection makes the association structural: the menu is created from the toplevel, dies with it, and arrives in order with the rest of that window's state.
What that costs is having to define a menu model here, which the rest of this file is. It is a flat set of nodes addressed by client-assigned id and linked by parent — a tree, expressed the way a tree survives being mutated incrementally.
Interoperating with toolkits that already speak D-Bus menus is a bridge over this protocol, and deliberately not a second path through it.
Warning! This protocol is Trinix's own and is not stable.

request.name: destroy
request.description: Menus created from it are unaffected.

request.name: get_menu_bar
request.description: The menu bar is shown while the toplevel is active, and hidden when it is not. It is a protocol error to ask for a second menu bar for the same toplevel.

entry.name: already_has_menu
entry.summary: the toplevel already exported a menu bar

entry.name: bad_item
entry.summary: an item id was zero, duplicated, or unknown

entry.name: bad_parent
entry.summary: the parent id is not a submenu

interface.name: trinix_menu_v1
interface.description:
Changes are accumulated and applied atomically by `commit`, for the same reason surface state is: a menu that is half-rebuilt must never be a menu the user can see, let alone click.
Item ids are chosen by the client, must be non-zero, and must be unique within this menu. Id 0 is the menu bar itself, and is the parent of the top-level menus.
A client is free to describe the whole menu up front, or to describe only the bar and fill each menu in when `about_to_show` arrives. The second is what an application with a large or expensive menu should do, and the protocol is shaped so that it costs nothing extra.

request.name: insert
request.description: `index` is the position among `parent`'s existing children; a negative index appends. Inserting an item whose id already exists is a protocol error — use `update`.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: client-assigned, non-zero, unique in this menu

arg.name: label
arg.summary: with an underscore before the mnemonic, if any

request.name: update
request.description: Keeps the item's identity, its position and its children, which is what makes it safe to call on every state change without the open menu flickering.

request.name: set_accelerator

description.summary: give an item a keyboard shortcut

request.description:
The shell both displays this and honours it: a shortcut on a menu item works whether or not the menu has ever been opened, which is the behaviour users expect and the reason the shell needs to know about it rather than the application handling the key itself.
A keysym of zero removes the accelerator.

description.summary: delete an item and its children

request.name: commit

description.summary: apply everything since the last commit

request.description: A commit with no pending changes is valid and does nothing.

event.name: activated
event.description: Sent for leaf items only. For a checkbox or a radio item the client is responsible for deciding the new state and sending `update`: the shell does not assume a click toggles anything, because whether it does is the application's business.

event.name: about_to_show

description.summary: a submenu is about to open

event.description: The client may mutate the menu and commit; the shell shows the menu on the next commit, or immediately if none arrives promptly. An application that populates lazily should do it here.

event.name: closed
event.description: Nothing is open any more, whether because the user chose something or because they dismissed it.

entry.name: checkbox
entry.summary: an item with an independent on/off state

entry.name: radio
entry.summary: one of a set; siblings of the same kind are exclusive

entry.name: checked
entry.summary: ticked, for a checkbox or radio item

entry.name: hidden
entry.summary: present in the model but not shown
